name: How performance scales with model and data size
gist: Understanding the mathematical relationship between performance and scale: how much better do models get as you make them bigger or give them more training data.
explain: When you double the amount of training data, does your model get twice as good? When you double the number of weights in the network, how much better are predictions? These scaling questions matter enormously because they determine how much data and compute you need to reach acceptable performance. Yet scaling is not straightforward. Sometimes doubling data gives almost no improvement because the model has already learned all the variety in the current data, leaving nothing new to find. Sometimes doubling the model size hurts performance because the larger model overfits — it memorizes noise rather than finding patterns. This subtheme investigates: what is the mathematical relationship between model size, data size, and performance?

The difficulty is that scaling depends on many factors: the problem you are solving (some tasks are intrinsically harder than others), the model architecture (some designs scale better than others), the algorithm (training methods matter), and the data itself (are you doubling data diversity or just repetition?), so each factor compounds in unpredictable ways. In the deep learning era, empirically observed scaling laws predict performance from a formula involving model size and data size, yet these are primarily empirical observations without deep theoretical justification, meaning practitioners cannot explain why or when they break. Additionally, scaling is not always monotonic — sometimes a larger model trained on more data performs worse, possibly due to interaction between architectural choices and learning dynamics, which means you cannot assume that more of everything is better. Understanding when scaling helps and when it hurts requires analyzing what happens inside the learning algorithm because this analysis reveals the mechanism, so you can predict whether more scale will improve or degrade outcomes, which guides investment decisions in infrastructure.

Researchers study sample complexity — how many examples must you show a model to achieve a target performance level — for different learning problems and algorithms, because this tells you the minimum data required to trust the model. They analyze convergence rates, predicting how quickly an algorithm improves as it processes more data, because this speed tells you how much training data is worth collecting, so you know when you have collected enough or when diminishing returns set in. They examine overfitting curves, which show performance improving on training data but degrading on test data as models grow too complex, so you can spot when a model is memorizing noise rather than learning patterns. They also study the practical phenomenon of double descent: as you increase model capacity past the point where the model can memorize all training data, performance first gets worse (overfitting), then gets better again (the larger model can express simpler, more generalizable solutions), which contradicts the conventional wisdom that you should minimize model size because it shows complexity does not always hurt, suggesting that the relationship between complexity and generalization is more nuanced than previously believed. This suggests that bigger models, when trained correctly, can generalize better despite the risk of overfitting because the mechanism learned via double descent overcomes overfitting, which explains why modern large models work better than theory predicts and motivates why practitioners now build larger models rather than smaller ones to achieve better real-world performance. The field also investigates Pareto-optimal frontiers, showing tradeoffs between model size (computational cost) and accuracy, helping practitioners choose models that perform well given their compute budget.

papers.title: Active Budget Allocation for Efficient Scaling Law Estimation via Surrogate-Guided Pruning
papers.contribution: Mean relative improvements of up to 5.47% on synthetic datasets while saving up to 98.7% computational cost compared to exhaustive approaches.

papers.title: Dropout Universality: Scaling Laws and Optimal Scheduling at the Edge-of-Chaos
papers.contribution: Front-loaded dropout schedules cut test loss by 18-35% over constant dropout in MLPs and Vision Transformers with no additional cost.

papers.title: Larger Datasets Can Be Repeated More: A Theoretical Analysis of Multi-Epoch Scaling in Linear Regression
papers.contribution: Proves that small K yields linear gains (E ≈ K) while larger K plateaus at problem-dependent values Θ(log N), explaining why larger datasets can be repeated more before marginal benefit vanishes.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Precision in High-Dimensional Linear Regression
papers.contribution: Shows multiplicative quantization preserves effective model size while additive quantization reduces it, providing principled basis for optimizing training under hardware constraints.

papers.title: Scaling Laws of SignSGD in Linear Regression: When Does It Outperform SGD?
papers.contribution: signSGD can achieve steeper compute-optimal slopes than SGD in noise-dominant regimes, and the warmup-stable-decay schedule further reduces noise and sharpens the optimal slope.

papers.title: Single-Head Attention in High Dimensions: A Theory of Generalization, Weights Spectra, and Scaling Laws
papers.contribution: Predicts full singular-value distribution of trained query-key maps including low-rank structure and outliers, and demonstrates power-law scaling laws emerge from sequential spectral recovery.

papers.title: Why Less is More (Sometimes): A Theory of Data Curation
papers.contribution: Provides analytical conditions and exact phase transition curves; validates on ImageNet that curated datasets can outperform full datasets and mitigate model collapse.

papers.title: t-SNE Exaggerates Clusters, Provably
papers.contribution: Proves that t-SNE cannot reliably preserve input clustering strength or outlier extremity, demonstrating prevalence of these failure modes in practice.

papers.title: A Random Matrix Theory of Masked Self-Supervised Learning
papers.contribution: Proves BBP-type phase transitions for signal recovery and identifies structured regimes where masked SSL provably outperforms PCA.

papers.title: A universal compression theory: Lottery ticket hypothesis and superpolynomial scaling laws
papers.contribution: The compression theory establishes that large neural networks can be compressed to polylogarithmic width preserving learning dynamics, and datasets to polylogarithmic size preserving loss landscapes.

papers.title: Causal Representation Learning with Optimal Compression and Complex Treatments
papers.contribution: Significantly outperforms traditional models in estimation accuracy and efficiency, particularly in large-scale intervention scenarios while ensuring both accuracy and computational efficiency.

papers.title: Convex Dominance in Deep Learning I: A Scaling Law of Loss and Learning Rate
papers.contribution: Demonstrates learning rate scaling laws that extrapolate 80× across training horizons and 70× across model sizes.

papers.title: Critical attention scaling in long-context transformers
papers.contribution: Provides rigorous theoretical justification for logarithmic attention scaling used in YaRN and Qwen, explaining how it maintains sparse content-adaptive attention.

papers.title: Deriving Neural Scaling Laws from the Statistics of Natural Language
papers.contribution: Our theory exhibits a remarkable match with experimentally measured neural scaling laws obtained from training GPT-2 and LLaMA style models from scratch on two qualitatively different benchmarks, Tiny

papers.title: Explaining Data Mixing Scaling Laws
papers.contribution: The framework outperforms baselines in fitting loss landscapes and successfully extrapolates across scales to predict highly effective training mixtures.

papers.title: Fast Escape, Slow Convergence: Learning Dynamics of Phase Retrieval under Power-Law Data
papers.contribution: Provides first rigorous characterization of scaling laws in nonlinear regression with anisotropic power-law data.

papers.title: Finding the Minimal Parameter Budget for Implicit Reasoning: A Data Complexity Driven Scaling Law for Language Models
papers.contribution: Shows optimally sized models can reliably reason over approximately 0.008 bits of information per parameter, characterizing minimal sufficient capacity for implicit reasoning.

papers.title: Geometric Entropy and Retrieval Phase Transitions in Continuous Thermal Dense Associative Memory
papers.contribution: Shows maximum theoretical capacity alpha=0.5 at zero temperature; identifies qualitative differences between kernels: LSE exhibits critical line at all loads while LSR has threshold below which no spurious patterns exist.

papers.title: How much can language models memorize?
papers.contribution: Estimates GPT-style models have capacity of approximately 3.6 bits per parameter; models memorize until capacity fills then transition to generalization.

papers.title: Improved Scaling Laws via Weak-to-Strong Generalization in Random Features Ridge Regression
papers.contribution: Shows scaling law improvement is substantial and students may achieve minimax optimal rate regardless of teacher's scaling law.

papers.title: InfoLaw: Information Scaling Laws for Large Language Models with Quality-Weighted Mixture Data and Repetition
papers.contribution: Predicts performance on unseen recipes and larger runs (up to 7B, 425B tokens) with 0.15% mean and 0.96% max error; enables efficient data-recipe selection under varying budgets.

papers.title: InfoTok: Adaptive Discrete Video Tokenizer via Information-Theoretic Compression
papers.contribution: Saves 20% tokens without affecting performance and achieves 2.3x compression rates while still outperforming prior heuristic adaptive approaches.

papers.title: Inheriting Generalizable Knowledge from LLMs to Diverse Vertical Tasks
papers.contribution: MASA outperforms random initialization, pruning, and distillation on language understanding and dialogue tasks, enabling lightweight models to converge faster.

papers.title: Intrinsic Entropy of Context Length Scaling in LLMs
papers.contribution: The theoretical framework establishes that training dataset size dictates optimal context length and provides bounds on context length scaling.

papers.title: LLMs as Noisy Channels: A Shannon Perspective on Model Capacity and Scaling Laws
papers.contribution: The theory outperforms classical scaling laws and predicts unseen model sizes up to 307B tokens with R²=0.847, successfully capturing non-monotonic loss basins.

papers.title: Learning is Forgetting; LLM Training As Lossy Compression
papers.contribution: Compression optimality predicts downstream performance on MMLU-Pro across different model families, linking representational structure to actionable insights.

papers.title: On the Origin of Neural Scaling Laws: from Random Graphs to Natural Language
papers.contribution: Scaling laws emerge even without data power laws; scaling exponents depend on data complexity; results hold for random graphs and simplified language, demonstrating scaling laws are robust phenomena.

papers.title: Overparametrization bends the landscape: BBP transitions at initialization in simple Neural Networks
papers.contribution: Demonstrate that overparameterization 'bends' the loss landscape, shifting BBP transition points even reaching weak-recovery threshold in large overparameterization limit.

papers.title: Predictable Compression Failures: Order Sensitivity and Information Budgeting for Evidence-Grounded Binary Adjudication
papers.contribution: On 3,059 grounded items, ISR=1 gate achieves 0.0-0.7% hallucination with 20.6-27.9% abstention (95% CIs) without universal calibration claims.

papers.title: Random Scaling of Emergent Capabilities
papers.contribution: Demonstrates sharp metric breakthroughs are produced by underlying continuous distribution changes, appearing well before most seeds achieve breakthrough.

papers.title: Revisiting the Volume Hypothesis
papers.contribution: Shows generalization advantage of gradient learning over random sampling diminishes with larger training data, resolving apparent paradox.

papers.title: Risk Phase Transitions in Spiked Regression: Alignment Driven Benign and Catastrophic Overfitting
papers.contribution: Shows that increasing spike strength can surprisingly induce catastrophic overfitting before achieving benign overfitting, and identifies when target-spike alignment is detrimental.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Symmetry, Evidence from Neural Force Fields
papers.contribution: The analysis reveals that equivariance matters more at larger scales with architecture-dependent exponents, and data and model sizes should scale in tandem for compute-optimal training.

papers.title: Understanding Catastrophic Forgetting In LoRA via Mean-Field Attention Dynamics
papers.contribution: Characterizes regimes with phase transitions between forgetting and non-forgetting behavior with respect to perturbation norm and depth, bounding time-to-deviation in terms of perturbation size.

papers.title: Universal One-third Time Scaling in Learning Peaked Distributions
papers.contribution: Provides mechanistic explanation for observed neural scaling laws and suggests new directions for improving training efficiency.
